title: Nada (Ascent of Mount Carmel)
hook: his drawing of the mountain: nothing, nothing, nothing, and on the mountain, nothing

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah, where even our ideas of God are purified. Your line was bigger than your idea. Today, one small Spanish word, drawn on a mountain.

A friar sits down and draws a mountain for a convent of nuns. Paths wind up it, with words written along them. It's John, after his escape. He's been sent south, and in the town of Beas he visits the Carmelite nuns as their confessor and teacher. So he does something teachers still do: he draws a diagram. He makes copies and hands them out, so each nun can keep one in her breviary. And written again and again up the middle path is today's word.
screen: `A FRIAR DRAWS A MOUNTAIN.` → `FOR THE NUNS OF BEAS.` → `A COPY FOR EACH BREVIARY.`

segments.voice: First, the two wide roads. On the left and right of John's mountain are broad paths. One is labeled with the goods of earth: possessions, pleasure, knowledge, comfort. The other with the goods of heaven: glory, joy, consolation, even spiritual rewards. Both look sensible. Both wind around and stop short of the top. Second, the narrow way. Straight up the middle runs a thin path, and on it John writes one Spanish word, over and over: nada, nada, nada, nada. Nothing. And near the top: and even on the mountain, nothing. Third, the verses. Beside the drawing, and later in his book the Ascent of Mount Carmel, John writes lines that turn on this word. In his Spanish: "Para venir a gustarlo todo, no quieras tener gusto en nada." To come to enjoy everything, desire to have enjoyment in nothing. To come to possess everything, desire to possess nothing. To come to be everything, desire to be nothing. Fourth, what it means. It sounds bleak. It isn't meant to be. John isn't saying the world is bad, or that people don't matter. His point is about grasping. Cling to anything, even good things, even spiritual things, and your hands are full. Nada is emptying the hands. And the promise at the top of the drawing isn't nothing. It's everything, which is God. Nothing, then everything: the order is the lesson.
screen: `TWO WIDE ROADS STOP SHORT.` · `NADA, NADA, NADA UP THE MIDDLE.` · `TO ENJOY ALL, CLING TO NOTHING.` · `EMPTY HANDS, THEN EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `NO QUIERAS TENER GUSTO EN NADA.`

segments.voice: Open your hands on your knees, palms up, and think of one thing you've been wanting hard: a purchase, a result, someone's approval, even a certain feeling in prayer. Picture it resting in your open hands, and stop gripping; you don't have to throw it away. If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, notice how open hands feel.
Nada. Spanish for nothing, written up the narrow path on John's drawing of Mount Carmel: cling to nothing, and at the top, God, who is everything. Today's word.
Your line: nothing, then everything. Empty hands have room for what John promises at the top. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Carmelites and many Catholics study John's sketch of Mount Carmel and the nada verses from the Ascent, often as a guide to detachment in Lent or on retreat.

fork.setup: you're climbing John's mountain. one road promises comfort, another promises spiritual joys, and a thin path up the middle says nothing, nothing, nothing. which do you take?
fork.reveal: on John's drawing only the narrow path of nada reaches the top, where he promises everything, which is God.

original.note: Spanish: nothing. from Latin (res) nata, a thing born, used in 'not a thing'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy word about giving everything up.

what a scholar hears: the 'Monte de Perfección' sketch for the nuns of Beas; the todo and nada verses appear in Ascent of Mount Carmel 1.13.

chat.says: Was John of the Cross saying the world is bad and we should want nothing?
options: No, his point is grasping: cling to nothing, and the top of the path is everything, God.
Yes, he taught that people and the world are bad and should be avoided.
No, he meant only earthly goods; holding on to spiritual rewards is always safe.
chat.meaning: John isn't saying the world is bad. Clinging to anything, even spiritual things, fills your hands. Nada empties them for God, who is everything.
